title: The Empires Around Israel
summary: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome: when each ruled the land of Israel, how each governed, the kings the Bible names, and where each touches the biblical story, with the prophets' claim that all of them answered to Israel's God.

sections.h: A small land between great powers
sections.body:
The land of Israel is small: from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south is about 240 kilometers (150 miles), and from the Mediterranean to the Jordan about 80 kilometers (50 miles) at its widest. But it lies on the only land bridge between Africa and Asia, the narrow strip of habitable ground between the sea and the desert along which armies and caravans had to pass between Egypt and Mesopotamia. The great coastal road, later called the Via Maris, and the King's Highway east of the Jordan both ran through or beside it. Whoever wanted to rule the Near East had to control this corridor, and so for most of its history Israel lived in the shadow of an empire: Egypt to the southwest, Assyria and Babylon to the northeast across the Fertile Crescent, then Persia, then the Greek kingdoms, then Rome.

The Bible does not treat these empires as neutral background. It insists that they rose and fell under the hand of Israel's God, often as instruments they did not know they were. Isaiah calls Assyria “the rod of My anger” (Isaiah 10:5) and then condemns its king for boasting that he had done it all by his own strength (Isaiah 10:12-15). Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar “My servant” (Jeremiah 27:6). Isaiah names Cyrus the LORD's “anointed” (Isaiah 45:1). Daniel learns in Babylon itself “that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes” (Daniel 4:17). A reader who knows the empires can see how bold these claims were, made by a small and often conquered people about the superpowers of their day.

Besides the great empires, Israel lived among smaller neighbors that appear constantly in the story: the Philistines on the southern coast, the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon to the north, the Aramean kingdom of Damascus, and Ammon, Moab, and Edom east and south of the Dead Sea. For much of the ninth century Damascus was Israel's most dangerous enemy. This guide concentrates on the six great powers. The guides to the kings, to the time between the testaments, and to the Herods and governors give more detail on particular periods.

Egypt was the oldest of the great powers and the most constant. Its kingdom was united around 3000 BC and lasted, under native and foreign dynasties, for nearly three thousand years. Egyptologists divide its history into the Old Kingdom (the age of the great pyramids, about 2700 to 2200 BC), the Middle Kingdom (about 2050 to 1650), and the New Kingdom (about 1550 to 1070), when Egypt ruled Canaan as part of an empire reaching to the Euphrates. After that Egypt was weaker and often divided, but it remained a force that Israel's kings were tempted to lean on, against the prophets' warnings (Isaiah 30:1-5; 31:1).

The patriarchs went down to Egypt in famine; Joseph rose to power there; Israel grew into a people there and was enslaved. The date of the exodus is disputed. A date around 1446 BC follows from 1 Kings 6:1, which places the exodus 480 years before Solomon began the temple; it is defended by scholars such as Eugene Merrill and Bryant Wood. A date in the thirteenth century, under Ramesses II (about 1279 to 1213), draws on the mention of the store city ‘Rameses’ (Exodus 1:11), which recalls Ramesses II's capital Pi-Ramesses, and on the archaeology of Canaan; its defenders include Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier, who read the 480 years as a symbolic figure of twelve generations. Many critical scholars, such as Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman (The Bible Unearthed, 2001), doubt that an exodus happened on the scale the Bible describes. Whatever the date, the Merneptah Stele, erected around 1208 BC by Ramesses II's successor, contains the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible, as a people in Canaan.

Later pharaohs appear by name. Shishak (Shoshenq I) raided Judah and Israel around 925 (1 Kings 14:25). Hoshea of Israel sent to “King So of Egypt” (2 Kings 17:4), a ruler not certainly identified; Osorkon IV has been proposed, and some read the name as the city of Sais. Tirhakah (Taharqa), a king of the Nubian dynasty that ruled Egypt from Cush, marched against Sennacherib in 701 (2 Kings 19:9), apparently as a commander for the reigning king, since he became king himself only in 690; the Bible calls him by the title he later held. Pharaoh Neco II killed Josiah at Megiddo in 609 and was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish in 605 (Jeremiah 46:2). Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) sent an army that briefly lifted the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:5) and was later overthrown, as Jeremiah foretold (Jeremiah 44:30).

Egypt was also a refuge. After Jerusalem fell, a group of Judeans fled there and took Jeremiah with them (Jeremiah 43). By the fifth century a colony of Jewish soldiers served the Persians at Elephantine, an island on the Nile at Egypt's southern border, where they had their own temple; their Aramaic papyri, including a letter of 407 BC asking the governor of Judah for help to rebuild it, are an important window into the Persian period. Alexandria later held the largest Jewish community outside the land, where the Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek. And Matthew records that the holy family fled to Egypt from Herod (Matthew 2:13-15).

Assyria's heartland lay on the upper Tigris River in what is now northern Iraq, around the cities of Ashur, Calah (Nimrud), and Nineveh. Assyria was an old kingdom, but its great age, which historians call the Neo-Assyrian Empire, ran from about 911 to 609 BC. It was the first empire to rule the whole of the Near East from the Persian Gulf to Egypt, and it did so by a mix of treaties, tribute, and terror. Vassal kings swore loyalty oaths before the gods and paid yearly tribute; those who rebelled saw their cities burned, their leaders impaled or flayed, and their people deported to the other end of the empire, while foreigners were brought in to replace them. The palace reliefs from Nineveh and Nimrud, now largely in the British Museum, show these campaigns in detail, including the siege of Lachish in Judah in 701.

Assyria first touched Israel in the ninth century, when Shalmaneser III fought a coalition that included Ahab at Qarqar in 853 and received Jehu's tribute in 841. The decisive century was the eighth. Tiglath-pileser III (745 to 727), called Pul in 2 Kings 15:19, turned raiding into annexation: he took tribute from Menahem, took Galilee and Gilead from Pekah and deported their people (2 Kings 15:29), and received Ahaz of Judah as a willing vassal (2 Kings 16:7-10). Shalmaneser V (727 to 722) besieged Samaria, which fell in 722, and Sargon II (722 to 705) deported its people and brought settlers from Babylonia and Syria in their place (2 Kings 17:5-6, 24). The Samaritans of the New Testament descend in part from the people of this mixed region.

Sennacherib (705 to 681) invaded Judah in 701 when Hezekiah rebelled. His annals, preserved on clay prisms, claim forty-six fortified cities of Judah taken and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and they record a heavy tribute; they do not claim that Jerusalem fell. The Bible tells of the tribute (2 Kings 18:14-16) and of the angel of the LORD striking the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:35-36). Sennacherib was murdered by two of his sons (2 Kings 19:37), which Assyrian and Babylonian records confirm. Under Esarhaddon (681 to 669) and Ashurbanipal (669 to about 631) Assyria reached its greatest extent, even conquering Egypt and sacking Thebes in 663, and Manasseh of Judah appears in their records as a loyal vassal. Ezra 4:10 remembers ‘Osnappar’, usually identified with Ashurbanipal, as a king who settled deportees in Samaria.

Then the empire collapsed with startling speed. The Babylonians under Nabopolassar and the Medes took Ashur in 614 and Nineveh in 612; the last Assyrian king fell back to Harran and was driven out in 610 and 609. Nahum's prophecy celebrates the fall of Nineveh, and the book of Jonah tells of an earlier moment when the great city repented at a prophet's preaching, a story that made Assyria, of all nations, the object of God's mercy.

sections.body:
Babylon, on the Euphrates south of modern Baghdad, was the ancient cultural capital of Mesopotamia, the city of Hammurabi and of the god Marduk. Under Assyrian rule it rebelled repeatedly; Merodach-baladan (Marduk-apla-iddina II), a Chaldean leader who held Babylon's throne twice against Assyria, sent envoys to Hezekiah (2 Kings 20:12-19; Isaiah 39), no doubt seeking allies. In 626 another Chaldean, Nabopolassar, made Babylon independent, and with the Medes he destroyed Assyria. The Neo-Babylonian Empire, also called the Chaldean Empire, lasted less than ninety years, but in that time it ended the kingdom of Judah.

Its great king was Nebuchadnezzar II (605 to 562). As crown prince he defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish in 605, and in the same year took the first captives from Jerusalem, among them, according to the book of Daniel, Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1:1-6). When Jehoiakim rebelled, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem; the Babylonian Chronicle records that he took the city on the second of Adar in his seventh year, 16 March 597, captured its king, and appointed a king of his own choosing, whom the Bible names as Zedekiah. When Zedekiah rebelled in turn, the Babylonians besieged the city for about eighteen months, broke through in 587 or 586, and burned the temple (2 Kings 25). Jeremiah 52:28-30 lists three deportations, including one in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year (582). Nebuchadnezzar also rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale; the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate from his city now stands reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.

The exiles were not scattered as slaves but settled in communities, mostly in the countryside near Nippur, along the canals ‘by the rivers of Babylon’ (Psalm 137:1). Jeremiah wrote to them to build houses, plant gardens, and “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles” (Jeremiah 29:7). Cuneiform tablets from a village called Al-Yahudu, ‘Judah-town’, published in 2014 by Laurie Pearce and Cornelia Wunsch, record Judean families there buying, leasing, and paying taxes across several generations. Ration tablets from Babylon list oil for the exiled King Jehoiachin, whom Nebuchadnezzar's son Amel-Marduk (Evil-merodach) released from prison (2 Kings 25:27-30).

The last Babylonian king, Nabonidus (556 to 539), spent about ten years at the oasis of Tayma in Arabia and left his son Belshazzar in charge at Babylon. This explains why Belshazzar in Daniel 5 could offer Daniel only the third place in the kingdom (Daniel 5:29): he himself was second. Babylon fell to the Persian king Cyrus in 539, almost without a fight, an event recorded in the Nabonidus Chronicle and on the Cyrus Cylinder. The ‘Darius the Mede’ who receives the kingdom in Daniel 5:31 is not known from other sources. He has been identified with Cyrus's governor Gubaru (by John Whitcomb, Darius the Mede, 1959), with Cyrus himself (by D. J. Wiseman, reading Daniel 6:28 as ‘Darius, that is, Cyrus’), or, by many critical scholars, taken as a figure built from later memories of Darius I. In later Jewish and Christian writing, Babylon became the name for any proud power opposed to God: Peter writes from ‘Babylon’, very likely meaning Rome (1 Peter 5:13), and Revelation announces, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great” (Revelation 18:2).

sections.body:
Cyrus II, called Cyrus the Great, united the Medes and Persians in the 550s, conquered the wealthy kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor in the 540s, and took Babylon in 539. His empire, the Achaemenid Persian Empire (named for its royal family), became the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from Egypt and the Aegean to the Indus. Persia governed differently from Assyria and Babylon. It divided the empire into large provinces called satrapies, ruled through local elites, used Aramaic as the common language of administration, and allowed, even sponsored, the worship of local gods. The Cyrus Cylinder, found in the ruins of Babylon in 1879, records Cyrus returning captured gods to their shrines and letting deported peoples go home. It does not mention the Jews, but it shows the policy under which Cyrus's decree in Ezra 1:1-4, issued in his first year over Babylon (538), makes sense.

The returned exiles lived in the small province of Yehud (Judah) within the satrapy the Bible calls ‘Beyond the River’, the lands west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:10). Under Darius I (522 to 486), with the encouragement of Haggai and Zechariah, they finished the second temple in his sixth year, 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Xerxes I (486 to 465), the king whose invasion of Greece ended in defeat at Salamis in 480, is the Ahasuerus of the book of Esther, called Xerxes in the BSB. Artaxerxes I (465 to 424) sent Ezra to Jerusalem in his seventh year, most likely 458, and Nehemiah as governor in his twentieth, 445 (Ezra 7:7-8; Nehemiah 2:1). Some scholars, following Albin van Hoonacker in the 1890s, date Ezra instead to the seventh year of Artaxerxes II, 398, which would put Nehemiah first; the traditional order still has many defenders. The Aramaic chapters of Ezra (4:8 to 6:18 and 7:12-26) preserve Persian-style official correspondence in the empire's own administrative language.

The Persian period was the time in which much of the Old Testament took its final shape and the Jewish community learned to live as a people of the Law under foreign rule. It ended when Alexander the Great defeated Darius III in 333 and 331. Daniel's visions of a ram with two horns (the kings of Media and Persia) overthrown by a goat from the west (Greece) are explained in the text itself (Daniel 8:20-21).

sections.body:
Alexander of Macedon became king in 336 BC at the age of twenty. In eleven years he conquered the whole Persian Empire: he defeated the Persians at the Granicus (334) and Issus (333), took Tyre after a seven-month siege and Gaza after two months (332), entered Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, and broke Darius III at Gaugamela (331). He reached the Indus before his army refused to go farther, and he died at Babylon in 323, not yet thirty-three. Judea passed under his rule in 332 without a battle. Josephus tells a story of Alexander bowing before the high priest in Jerusalem (Antiquities 11.329-339), which most historians regard as legend.

His generals divided the empire. Two of their dynasties matter for the Bible. The Ptolemies ruled Egypt from Alexandria, and the Seleucids ruled Syria and Mesopotamia from Antioch. Judea lay between them, and Daniel 11 traces their wars in detail as the struggles of ‘the king of the South’ and ‘the king of the North’. The Ptolemies held Judea for a century, until the Seleucid Antiochus III won it at the battle of Panium around 200 BC. His son Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 to 164) tried to force Greek religion on Jerusalem, desecrated the temple in 167, and provoked the Maccabean revolt. The guide to the time between the testaments in this series tells that story.

Greek rule changed the world into which the New Testament was born more deeply than any conquest before it. Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean, which is why the New Testament was written in Greek, even by Jews of Galilee and Judea, and why a Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, the Septuagint, was made in Alexandria from the third century BC onward. Greek cities were founded or refounded across the region, among them the ten cities of the Decapolis that Jesus visited (Mark 5:20; 7:31). Greek education, athletics, philosophy, and religion pressed on Jewish life everywhere, and Jews responded in every way from eager adoption to armed resistance.

Rome grew from a city-state in Italy into the ruler of the whole Mediterranean over three centuries of war. It defeated Carthage and the Greek kingdoms, and its influence reached Judea when the Maccabees made a treaty with the Roman Senate (1 Maccabees 8). In 63 BC the Roman general Pompey, called in to settle a Hasmonean civil war, took Jerusalem and entered the Most Holy Place of the temple. From then on Judea was under Roman power, first through client rulers such as Herod the Great, later through Roman governors. After a century of civil wars, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, and in 27 BC took the name Augustus, becoming the first emperor.

The Roman peace (pax Romana) that followed made the spread of the gospel possible in practical ways. Roman roads, Roman suppression of piracy, a common coinage, and the use of Greek across the eastern provinces let Paul travel from Antioch to Corinth to Rome. Roman citizenship, which Paul held from birth (Acts 22:28), protected him from flogging without trial and gave him the right to appeal to Caesar (Acts 25:11). Roman governors appear at every turn in Acts, and some are known from outside the Bible: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12), appears in an inscription at Delphi that dates his term to about 51 or 52.

Rome also executed Jesus by crucifixion, its penalty for slaves and rebels, and later persecuted the church. Nero blamed Christians for the great fire of Rome in 64 and put many to death, as Tacitus records (Annals 15.44). The Jewish revolt that began in 66 ended in AD 70, when Titus took Jerusalem and burned the temple; the Arch of Titus in Rome still shows the temple's lampstand carried in triumph. A second revolt, led by Simon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba) in 132 to 135, ended with Jerusalem refounded as a pagan colony, Aelia Capitolina, and Jews barred from it.

The New Testament speaks of Rome in two registers. Paul tells the church in Rome that governing authorities are “appointed by God” (Romans 13:1), and Peter tells believers to “fear God, honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). Revelation, written to churches under pressure to take part in the worship of the emperor, portrays the same empire as a beast from the sea and as Babylon the great, drunk with the blood of the saints (Revelation 13; 17 to 18). Most interpreters see these as two sides of one conviction: the state has real authority under God and becomes monstrous when it demands the worship that belongs to God alone.

The table summarizes the six powers, when each dominated the land of Israel, and where each touches the story. The dates of dominance over Israel are shorter than the lifespans of the empires themselves: Egypt existed long before and after its rule over Canaan, and Rome lasted in the west until the fifth century AD and in the east, as the Byzantine Empire, until 1453.

Daniel's visions of four kingdoms (Daniel 2 and 7) are read in two main ways. The older Christian reading, found in Jerome and followed by many conservative interpreters, takes the four as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome, with God's kingdom arriving in the days of Rome. Many modern scholars, reading Daniel as completed in the second century BC, take them as Babylon, Media, Persia, and Greece, with the climax in the persecution of Antiochus IV. Both readings agree on the vision's central claim: that “the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44), outlasting every empire in the table.
